questions.text: Which planet in our solar system rotates clockwise (retrograde rotation) on its axis, causing the Sun to rise in the west?
questions.explanation: Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets in our solar system, taking 243 Earth days to complete a single rotation.

questions.text: What is the name of the tallest known volcano and mountain in the Solar System, located on Mars?
questions.explanation: Olympus Mons is a shield volcano on Mars standing roughly 21.9 km (13.6 miles) high, nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.

questions.text: Approximately how long does it take for light from the Sun to reach Earth?
questions.explanation: Traveling at roughly 299,792 km/s across 149.6 million km, sunlight takes about 499 seconds (8 minutes 19 seconds) to reach Earth.
questions.optionsJson: ["8 minutes and 20 seconds", "1 minute and 15 seconds", "24 minutes", "4.2 seconds"]

questions.text: Which moon of Saturn is the only moon in the solar system known to have a dense atmosphere and liquid hydrocarbon lakes on its surface?
questions.explanation: Titan has a thick nitrogen-rich atmosphere and surface lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

questions.text: What type of stellar remnant is formed when a massive star collapses into an ultra-dense core that spins up to hundreds of times per second?
questions.explanation: Pulsars are highly magnetized rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation out of their magnetic poles.

questions.text: Which spacecraft, launched in 1977, became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space in 2012?
questions.explanation: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause into interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to transmit data from beyond the solar system.

questions.text: What is the boundary around a black hole beyond which no light or matter can escape?
questions.explanation: Once matter or radiation crosses the event horizon, the gravitational pull requires an escape velocity exceeding the speed of light.

questions.text: Which star system is the closest known neighbor to our Solar System?
questions.explanation: The Alpha Centauri triple-star system, specifically Proxima Centauri at about 4.24 light-years away, is the closest star system to the Sun.

questions.text: Why do footprints left by Apollo astronauts on the Moon remain preserved for millions of years?
options: The Moon has no wind or liquid water to erode them
Lunar soil hardens into solid rock in sunlight
Solar magnetic fields lock dust particles in place
Earth's gravity shields the lunar surface
questions.explanation: Without an atmosphere, wind, or rain, only slow micrometeorite impacts alter the lunar regolith over geological timescales.
questions.optionsJson: ["The Moon has no wind or liquid water to erode them", "Lunar soil hardens into solid rock in sunlight", "Solar magnetic fields lock dust particles in place", "Earth's gravity shields the lunar surface"]

questions.text: Which planet has the shortest day in the Solar System, completing a full rotation in just under 10 hours?
questions.explanation: Despite being the largest planet, Jupiter spins once every 9 hours and 55 minutes, causing a noticeable equatorial bulge.

questions.text: What phenomenon causes two clean, uncoated pieces of the same metal to permanently fuse together in the vacuum of space?
questions.explanation: Without an oxide layer formed by atmospheric oxygen, metal atoms in direct contact share electrons and bond as a single piece.

questions.text: What is the largest moon in the Solar System, even larger in diameter than the planet Mercury?
questions.explanation: Orbiting Jupiter, Ganymede has a diameter of 5,268 km, making it larger than Mercury (4,879 km) and Pluto.

questions.text: Which chemical element is the only metal that is liquid at standard room temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: Mercury melts at -38.83°C (-37.89°F). Bromine is also liquid at room temperature, but it is a halogen non-metal.

questions.text: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the exact same numerical value?
questions.explanation: Using F = (9/5)C + 32, substituting -40 yields (-40 × 1.8) + 32 = -72 + 32 = -40.

questions.text: What is the term for the thermodynamic point where a substance can coexist as a solid, liquid, and gas simultaneously in equilibrium?
questions.explanation: At a substance's specific triple point temperature and pressure, all three phases exist in stable thermodynamic equilibrium.

questions.text: Why does helium make a person's voice sound higher in pitch when inhaled?
options: Sound travels faster through lighter helium gas, changing vocal tract resonance
Helium temporarily tightens the vocal cords
Helium increases the frequency of vocal fold vibrations
questions.explanation: The pitch of the vocal cords themselves does not change; rather, higher resonant frequencies are amplified because sound travels nearly 3 times faster in helium.
questions.optionsJson: ["Sound travels faster through lighter helium gas, changing vocal tract resonance", "Helium temporarily tightens the vocal cords", "Helium increases the frequency of vocal fold vibrations", "Helium cools the larynx"]

questions.text: Which abundant gas makes up approximately 78% of Earth's dry atmosphere by volume?
questions.explanation: Earth's dry atmosphere is roughly 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, and 0.04% carbon dioxide.

questions.text: What name is given to the counterintuitive observation that hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water under certain conditions?
questions.explanation: Named after Tanzanian student Erasto Mpemba in 1963, the Mpemba effect describes circumstances where warmer water freezes more rapidly than colder water.

questions.text: What causes a water droplet to skitter across a pan heated well above water's boiling point instead of evaporating instantly?
questions.explanation: In the Leidenfrost effect, the bottom of the droplet vaporizes immediately, creating an insulating cushion of steam that slows heat transfer.

questions.text: Which subatomic particle was predicted by Peter Higgs in 1964 and confirmed at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012?
questions.explanation: The Higgs boson is the quantum excitation of the Higgs field, which gives mass to fundamental particles.

questions.text: What property of diamonds makes them feel colder to the touch than glass at the same room temperature?
questions.explanation: Diamond conducts heat away from your fingers roughly five times faster than copper, making it feel icy to the touch.
questions.optionsJson: ["Exceptionally high thermal conductivity", "Lower specific density", "Reflective crystal facets", "Piezoelectric cooling"]

questions.text: Which radioactive element was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898 and named after Marie's homeland?
questions.explanation: Polonium (atomic number 84) was named after Poland, where Marie Skłodowska-Curie was born.

questions.text: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance known on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness?
questions.explanation: Diamond defines 10 on the Mohs hardness scale due to its rigid three-dimensional lattice of covalent carbon-carbon bonds.

questions.text: Why does pure water NOT conduct electricity well compared to tap water or seawater?
options: It lacks dissolved ions to carry electric charge
questions.explanation: Electrical conductivity in water depends on dissolved mineral ions (electrolytes); ultra-pure deionized water is actually a poor conductor.
questions.optionsJson: ["It lacks dissolved ions to carry electric charge", "Water molecules repel electrons", "Hydrogen bonds block magnetic fields", "Oxygen atoms absorb current"]

questions.text: Which ancient artifact, discovered in 1799 with inscriptions in three scripts, provided the key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs?
questions.explanation: Because the Rosetta Stone featured the same decree in Ancient Greek, Demotic, and Hieroglyphs, Jean-François Champollion was able to crack the hieroglyphic code in 1822.

questions.text: What was the purpose of the Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a Roman-era shipwreck off a Greek island in 1901?
options: An analog mechanical computer for tracking astronomical positions and eclipses
A hydraulic water clock for senate speeches
A gyroscopic compass for Mediterranean navigation
A cipher wheel for military dispatches
questions.explanation: Dating to around the 2nd century BCE, the Antikythera mechanism used at least 30 bronze gears to predict planetary motions and eclipse cycles.
questions.optionsJson: ["An analog mechanical computer for tracking astronomical positions and eclipses", "A hydraulic water clock for senate speeches", "A gyroscopic compass for Mediterranean navigation", "A cipher wheel for military dispatches"]

questions.text: Why has Ancient Roman marine concrete in harbor piers endured for over 2,000 years while modern concrete often degrades in decades?
options: Seawater reacts with volcanic ash and lime to grow interlocking mineral crystals
Romans reinforced piers with solid bronze rods
Roman harbors only used carved granite blocks without mortar
Ancient concrete was coated in beeswax
questions.explanation: Seawater percolating through Roman pozzolanic concrete dissolves volcanic ash and forms aluminum tobermorite crystals that heal micro-cracks.
questions.optionsJson: ["Seawater reacts with volcanic ash and lime to grow interlocking mineral crystals", "Romans reinforced piers with solid bronze rods", "Roman harbors only used carved granite blocks without mortar", "Ancient concrete was coated in beeswax"]

questions.text: Which civilization built the citadel of Machu Picchu high in the Andes Mountains in the 15th century?
questions.explanation: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 CE as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti in modern-day Peru.

questions.text: Which famous university in England was already teaching students more than 200 years before the Aztec Empire founded Tenochtitlan in 1325?
questions.explanation: Teaching at Oxford existed as early as 1096 CE, whereas the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 CE.
questions.optionsJson: ["University of Oxford", "University of Cambridge", "Durham University", "University of London"]

questions.text: How long did the Anglo-Zanzibar War of August 27, 1896—the shortest recorded war in history—last?
questions.explanation: The conflict between the United Kingdom and the Zanzibar Sultanate began at 9:02 AM and ended by 9:40 AM.

questions.text: What ancient writing system of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablet's originated in Mesopotamia around 3200 BCE?
questions.explanation: Developed by the Sumerians, cuneiform used a reed stylus to press wedge-shaped impressions into soft clay.

questions.text: Which spice was once so prized in medieval Europe and the Maluku Islands that the Dutch traded the island of Manhattan to the British in 1667 to secure a monopoly on it?
questions.explanation: In the Treaty of Breda (1667), the Dutch ceded New Amsterdam (Manhattan) while keeping Run Island in the Banda archipelago for its nutmeg trees.

questions.text: What archaeological site in southeastern Turkey, dating back to around 9500 BCE, features massive carved T-shaped limestone pillars built by hunter-gatherers?
questions.explanation: Göbekli Tepe predates Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids by roughly 6,000 years.

questions.text: Which ruler of the Mali Empire made a 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca distributing so much gold that it depressed gold prices in Cairo for a decade?
questions.explanation: Mansa Musa I ruled the gold-rich Mali Empire in the 14th century and became legendary across the Mediterranean world for his immense wealth.

questions.text: In what ancient Chinese dynasty was the Terracotta Army constructed to guard the tomb of China's first emperor?
questions.explanation: Thousands of life-sized terracotta soldiers were buried around 210 BCE with Qin Shi Huang, the founder of the Qin dynasty.

questions.text: Which ancient wonder of the world was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years until 1311 CE?
questions.explanation: Originally standing 146.6 meters (481 feet) tall, the Great Pyramid of Giza held the record until Lincoln Cathedral's central spire was completed in 1311.
questions.optionsJson: ["Great Pyramid of Giza", "Lighthouse of Alexandria", "Colossus of Rhodes", "Hanging Gardens of Babylon"]

questions.text: How many hearts does an octopus have, and what color is its blood?
questions.explanation: Octopuses have two branchial hearts to pump blood through their gills, one systemic heart for the body, and copper-based hemocyanin that turns their blood blue.
questions.optionsJson: ["Three hearts and blue blood", "Two hearts and red blood", "Four hearts and green blood", "One heart and clear blood"]

questions.text: Which microscopic animal can survive the vacuum of outer space, temperatures near absolute zero, and radiation thousands of times lethal to humans?
questions.explanation: Tardigrades enter a dehydrated state called cryptobiosis, suspending their metabolism to survive extreme environments.

questions.text: What is the deepest known point in Earth's oceans, located in the western Pacific Ocean?

questions.optionsJson: ["Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench", "Tonga Trench", "Puerto Rico Trench", "Java Trench"]

questions.text: Which bird holds the record for the longest annual migration, flying up to 70,000 km (44,000 miles) from pole to pole?
questions.explanation: The Arctic Tern migrates between the Arctic and Antarctic every year, experiencing two summers a year and more daylight than any other creature.

questions.text: Which mammal is one of the very few venomous mammals, with males possessing ankle spurs that deliver excruciating venom?
questions.explanation: Male platypuses have hollow spurs on their hind legs connected to crural glands that produce venom during the breeding season.

questions.text: Why are wild flamingos pink rather than white, the color they are when they hatch?

questions.text: Why was the standard QWERTY keyboard layout originally arranged the way it is in the 1870s?

To minimize finger movement to zero on the top row

questions.text: Why can't your brain feel pain if the brain tissue itself is touched during awake neurosurgery?

questions.explanation: Oxygen gets all the attention because we breathe it. Nitrogen makes up over three-quarters of every breath you take and you never notice it.

questions.text: Which element has the chemical symbol 'Au'?
questions.explanation: From the Latin 'aurum,' meaning 'shining dawn.' Most element symbols map obviously to their English names. Gold, silver (Ag), and a handful of others break the pattern.

questions.text: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.explanation: About 3 mm long. Smaller than a grain of rice. It transmits sound vibrations to the inner ear, and most people have never heard of it.

questions.text: What force keeps planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.explanation: Sounds obvious. Then someone says 'centrifugal force' and suddenly half the room is second-guessing themselves. Gravity pulls planets inward; their orbital velocity keeps them from falling in. No outward force needed.

questions.text: How many chromosomes do humans have?
questions.explanation: The trap here is the number 23, which floats around in pop culture. That's the number of pairs, not the total count. Double it.

questions.text: What organ in the human body produces insulin?
questions.explanation: Specifically the beta cells in the islets of Langerhans. The liver gets picked often because it handles so many metabolic functions, but insulin production belongs to the pancreas alone.

questions.text: What is the chemical formula for table salt?
questions.explanation: One of the first formulas taught in chemistry and one of the first forgotten. H₂O steals the spotlight.

questions.text: What is the speed of light in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: Everyone knows 'the speed of light' as a concept. Ask for the actual number and watch the confidence evaporate. The round approximation is 300,000 km/s, but the precise figure is 299,792,458 m/s.

questions.text: What gas do plants absorb from the atmosphere during photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Simple enough for a fifth grader, yet it trips adults who overthink it. Oxygen is what plants release, not what they absorb. The confusion runs both directions.

questions.text: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?
questions.explanation: From the Latin 'kalium,' via the Arabic 'al-qalyah' (plant ashes). English speakers expect 'P' or 'Po,' but P is phosphorus and Po is polonium.

questions.text: What percentage of the human body is water?
questions.explanation: Ranges from 45% to 75% depending on age and body composition. The classic '60%' figure applies to an average adult male. Newborns are closer to 75%.

questions.text: What is the largest desert in the world?
questions.explanation: Nearly everyone says the Sahara. A desert is defined by precipitation, not temperature. Antarctica receives less than 200 mm of precipitation per year and covers 14 million km², making it almost twice the size of the Sahara.

questions.text: Which country has the most time zones?
questions.explanation: France's overseas territories span the globe: French Polynesia, New Caledonia, Réunion, Martinique, and more. Russia, with 11 time zones across one contiguous landmass, comes second.

questions.text: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.explanation: Sydney and Melbourne compete for everything in Australia, including the wrong answer to this question. Canberra was built as a compromise capital specifically because the two cities couldn't stop arguing.

questions.text: What is the deepest point in the ocean?
questions.explanation: Deeper than Mount Everest is tall. Only four people have ever been to the bottom. The pressure down there is over 1,000 atmospheres.

questions.text: Which continent has the most countries?
questions.explanation: Asia is bigger by area and population, so it gets picked often. But Africa has 54 recognized sovereign states, beating Asia's 49.

questions.text: Which lake is the deepest in the world?
questions.explanation: Contains roughly 20% of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater. That single lake holds more water than all five Great Lakes combined.

questions.text: What is the longest mountain range on land?
questions.explanation: Runs through seven South American countries. The Rockies get picked by North Americans, the Himalayas by everyone else. Neither comes close in length.

questions.text: What is the smallest country in the world by area?
questions.explanation: Fits inside Rome's city limits. Monaco is the second smallest at 2.02 km², roughly five times larger. Some people confuse Monaco with Vatican City because both are European microstates.

questions.text: Which strait separates Africa from Europe?
questions.explanation: Only 14.3 km wide at its narrowest point. On a clear day you can see Morocco from Spain.
questions.optionsJson: ["Strait of Gibraltar", "Strait of Hormuz", "The Bosphorus", "Strait of Malacca"]

questions.text: Which river is the longest in the world?
questions.explanation: The Amazon gives it a serious fight depending on which tributaries you measure. By most accepted measurements, the Nile still wins by a narrow margin.

questions.text: What is the driest inhabited continent?
questions.explanation: Antarctica is drier, but 'inhabited' does the heavy lifting in this question. Australia's interior is vast desert, and even the populated coasts are surprisingly arid compared to other continents.

questions.text: What is the only continent with no active volcanoes?
questions.explanation: Sits in the middle of a tectonic plate rather than at its edges. No plate boundaries, no volcanic activity. The last eruption on the Australian mainland was over 5,000 years ago at Mount Gambier.

questions.text: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.explanation: 1991 gets picked often because that's when the Soviet Union dissolved. The Wall came down two years earlier. Two events, same era, constantly swapped.

questions.text: What ancient civilization built Machu Picchu?
questions.explanation: The Aztecs and Maya are the usual wrong answers. All three were pre-Columbian American civilizations, but only the Incas built in the Andes mountains of Peru.
questions.optionsJson: ["The Maya", "The Aztec Empire", "The Olmecs", "The Inca Empire"]

questions.text: Which war lasted from 1337 to 1453?
questions.explanation: Technically 116 years. The name is a round approximation that stuck. It was fought between England and France in a series of conflicts with long truces between them.
questions.optionsJson: ["The Wars of the Roses", "The Hundred Years' War", "The Thirty Years' War", "The Seven Years' War"]

questions.text: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci is the reflex answer for any Renaissance art question. Michelangelo spent four years on his back painting it. He considered himself a sculptor first and resented the commission.

questions.text: Which empire was ruled by Genghis Khan?
questions.explanation: At its peak, the largest contiguous land empire in history. Stretched from Korea to Hungary. People sometimes guess the Ottoman or Persian Empire because those names feel bigger.
questions.optionsJson: ["The Mongol Empire", "The Ottoman Empire", "The Persian Empire", "The Roman Empire"]

questions.text: In what year did World War I begin?
questions.explanation: 1939 gets blurted out by anyone whose brain auto-completes 'World War' with the second one. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in June 1914 triggered the first.

questions.text: What was the shortest war in history?
questions.explanation: Britain issued an ultimatum. Zanzibar didn't comply. The Royal Navy opened fire. Forty-five minutes later it was over. Barely long enough for a lunch break.
questions.optionsJson: ["The Anglo-Zanzibar War", "The Winter War", "The Six-Day War", "The Falklands War"]

questions.text: Which treaty ended World War I?
questions.explanation: Its harsh reparations against Germany are widely considered a contributing factor to World War II. The Armistice of November 11, 1918 stopped the fighting, but Versailles formally ended the war.
questions.optionsJson: ["The Peace of Westphalia", "The Treaty of Tordesillas", "The Treaty of Paris", "The Treaty of Versailles"]

questions.text: What was the name of the ship the Pilgrims sailed to America in 1620?
questions.explanation: Straightforward for Americans. Catches international players off guard. The voyage took 66 days and carried 102 passengers.
questions.optionsJson: ["The Endeavour", "The Santa Maria", "The Mayflower", "The Golden Hind"]

questions.text: Who wrote the 'I Have a Dream' speech?
questions.explanation: The 'dream' section was partially improvised. King departed from his prepared text, prompted by gospel singer Mahalia Jackson calling out 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!'
questions.optionsJson: ["Frederick Douglass", "Malcolm X", "Martin Luther King Jr.", "John F. Kennedy"]

questions.text: What ancient wonder was located in Alexandria, Egypt?
questions.explanation: The Library of Alexandria is more famous, but it wasn't one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The Lighthouse stood roughly 100 meters tall and guided ships for centuries.
questions.optionsJson: ["The Colossus of Rhodes", "The Lighthouse of Alexandria", "The Hanging Gardens of Babylon", "The Temple of Artemis"]

questions.text: What civilization built the Great Pyramid of Giza?
questions.explanation: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BCE for Pharaoh Khufu. It remained the tallest man-made structure on Earth for over 3,800 years.

questions.text: What is the largest organ in the human body?
questions.explanation: People reach for the liver or lungs. The skin covers about 1.7 square meters on an average adult and weighs around 3.6 kg. Hard to see it as an 'organ' when you're wearing it.

questions.text: How many squares are on a standard chessboard?
questions.explanation: Trick question territory. If you count all possible squares of all sizes, the answer is 204. But a standard board has 64 individual squares. The question's phrasing matters.

questions.text: What does the 'E' stand for in E = mc²?
questions.explanation: Einstein's most famous equation. The m is mass, c is the speed of light. Most people know the equation exists but freeze when asked what each letter represents.

questions.text: How many teeth does a typical adult human have?
questions.explanation: 28 is the common answer from people who've had their wisdom teeth removed and forgot to add them back.

questions.text: What is the most spoken language in the world by native speakers?
questions.explanation: English dominates as a second language, which is why it feels like the right answer. By native speakers alone, Mandarin leads with over 900 million.

questions.text: What is the smallest prime number?
questions.explanation: And the only even prime. People say 1, but 1 is not prime by mathematical convention. A prime must have exactly two distinct factors: 1 and itself. The number 1 has only one factor.

questions.text: What does DNA stand for?
questions.explanation: 'Deoxyribo-' is where everyone stumbles. The 'nucleic' part refers to the cell nucleus. Getting the full name right on the first try is rarer than you'd think.

questions.text: How many strings does a standard guitar have?
questions.explanation: Bass guitars have 4, twelve-string guitars exist, and ukuleles have 4. The standard acoustic or electric guitar: six strings. Simple, but the variations cause hesitation.

questions.text: What is the only letter that doesn't appear in any US state name?
questions.explanation: X appears in Texas and New Mexico. Z in Arizona. J in New Jersey. But Q? Not a single state uses it.

questions.text: Who invented the telephone?
questions.explanation: Antonio Meucci filed a caveat for a similar device five years earlier but couldn't afford the patent renewal fee. Elisha Gray filed his patent application the same day as Bell. The history is messier than the textbook version.

questions.text: What is the tallest building in the world?
questions.explanation: Completed in 2010 and still unbeaten in 2026. The Jeddah Tower in Saudi Arabia was designed to surpass it but has faced construction delays for years.

questions.text: In what language was the Bible's Old Testament primarily written?
questions.explanation: Greek is the common wrong answer, but that's the New Testament. The Old Testament was written primarily in Biblical Hebrew, with portions of Daniel and Ezra in Aramaic.

questions.text: How many continents are there?
questions.explanation: Depends on who you ask. The seven-continent model (Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia/Oceania, Europe, North America, South America) is standard in English-speaking countries. Some models count 5 or 6 by merging Europe and Asia, or the Americas.

questions.text: In which sport is the term 'love' used to mean zero?
questions.explanation: Comes from the French word 'l'oeuf' (egg), because a zero looks like an egg. At least, that's the popular theory. Linguists aren't fully convinced.

questions.text: How long is a marathon?
questions.explanation: The odd distance dates back to the 1908 London Olympics. The course was extended so it could start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box. That arbitrary extension became the permanent standard.

questions.text: Which country has won the most FIFA World Cup titles?
questions.explanation: Germany and Italy have 4 each. Argentina has 3. Brazil's five wins (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002) are the benchmark everyone chases.

questions.text: How many holes are in a standard round of golf?
questions.explanation: The Old Course at St Andrews originally had 22. In 1764 they combined several short holes, landing on 18, and it became the standard. Pure accident of Scottish course design.

questions.text: What is the national sport of Japan?
questions.explanation: Baseball is wildly popular in Japan, which is why it gets picked. But sumo holds the official title of national sport, rooted in Shinto ritual and centuries of tradition.

questions.text: In the Olympics, what do the five rings represent?
questions.explanation: Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. Pierre de Coubertin designed them in 1913. The colors (blue, yellow, black, green, red) were chosen because at least one appears in every nation's flag.
questions.optionsJson: ["Five ancient Greek city-states", "The five inhabited continents", "The five founding nations", "The five oceans"]

questions.text: How many points is a touchdown worth in American football?
questions.explanation: The extra point attempt after (worth 1 or 2) creates the illusion that touchdowns are worth 7. The touchdown itself: six points. Everything after is a separate play.

questions.text: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is played on clay courts?
questions.explanation: Wimbledon is grass, the US and Australian Opens are hard court. Clay slows the ball and produces higher bounces, which favors baseline players.
questions.optionsJson: ["Wimbledon", "The French Open", "The US Open", "The Australian Open"]

questions.text: In cricket, how many runs is a 'century'?
questions.explanation: Straightforward if you follow cricket. Complete mystery if you don't. A double century is 200, and a score of 99 is among the most agonizing things in the sport.

questions.text: How many players are on a standard soccer team on the field?
questions.explanation: Same as cricket, field hockey, and American football. The number 11 shows up across sports with suspicious regularity. Nobody planned this.

questions.text: What sport is played at Wimbledon?
questions.explanation: Formally 'The Championships, Wimbledon.' The oldest tennis tournament in the world, established in 1877. The all-white dress code still applies.

questions.text: Which athlete has won the most Olympic gold medals?
questions.explanation: Twenty-three golds across five Olympic Games (2000-2016). The next closest swimmer has 9. Phelps has more individual golds than most countries have golds total.

questions.text: What fruit is the main ingredient in guacamole?
questions.explanation: From the Nahuatl word 'ahuacamolli.' Some people say tomato because salsa looks similar, but guacamole is avocado-based with lime, cilantro, and salt.

questions.text: What is the main ingredient in hummus?
questions.explanation: The word 'hummus' literally means 'chickpeas' in Arabic. Tahini is the second key ingredient, but chickpeas do the heavy lifting.

questions.text: Which country produces the most coffee in the world?
questions.explanation: Has been the top producer for over 150 years. Produces roughly a third of the world's coffee. Colombia and Vietnam are distant second and third.

questions.text: What type of pasta is shaped like little ears?
questions.explanation: From the Italian 'orecchia' (ear) plus the diminutive '-ette.' Originates from Puglia in southern Italy. The small cup shape catches sauce beautifully.

questions.text: What gives bread its holes?
questions.explanation: Yeast eats sugar and produces CO₂ gas. The gas gets trapped in the gluten network, creating bubbles. When the bread bakes, the bubbles set in place. No yeast, no holes.
questions.optionsJson: ["Water evaporating", "Air whipped in by kneading", "Carbon dioxide from yeast", "Salt crystals"]

questions.text: What is the most consumed beverage in the world after water?
questions.explanation: Coffee drinkers are absolutely certain it's coffee. Tea wins by volume across China, India, and the rest of Asia. Coffee dominates the West but can't match tea's global reach.

questions.text: From which animal does venison come?
questions.explanation: The word sounds fancy enough that people guess exotic animals. In Old French, 'venaison' meant 'hunted meat' from any animal. Modern English narrowed it to deer.

questions.text: What nut is used to make marzipan?
questions.explanation: Ground almonds, sugar, and sometimes egg whites. Pistachios and cashews are common guesses, probably because marzipan's sweetness doesn't taste obviously almond-like.

questions.text: In which country did the croissant originate?
questions.explanation: The kipferl, a crescent-shaped pastry, was Austrian. French bakers later refined it with laminated dough (butter folded into layers). France perfected it, but Austria created it.

questions.text: What is the primary ingredient in tofu?
questions.explanation: Soy milk is coagulated and pressed into blocks. The process is similar to cheese-making. Rice gets guessed often, probably because tofu appears alongside rice so frequently.

questions.text: What country is the origin of sushi?
questions.explanation: Though the concept of preserving fish in fermented rice originated in Southeast Asia (likely modern-day China or Thailand). Japan transformed it into the fresh, vinegared-rice dish we know today.

questions.text: What spice gives curry its yellow color?
questions.explanation: Curry powder is a blend. Saffron is yellow too, which causes confusion. But turmeric is the workhorse pigment in most curry blends, and it costs a fraction of saffron's price.

questions.text: What is the name of Thor's hammer in Norse mythology?
questions.explanation: Pronounced roughly 'MYOL-nir.' Marvel movies made the name famous, but spelling it correctly still trips up most people.

questions.text: In Greek mythology, who turned people to stone with her gaze?
questions.explanation: One of three Gorgon sisters, and the only mortal one. Perseus killed her by using a mirrored shield to avoid direct eye contact. Her image became a protective symbol in ancient Greece.

questions.text: Who is the Norse god of mischief?
questions.explanation: Not actually a god in the traditional sense. Loki is a jötunn (giant) who lives among the Aesir gods. The Marvel version made him Thor's brother; the original myths make their relationship much more complicated.

questions.text: In Greek mythology, what was Achilles' only weakness?
questions.explanation: His mother Thetis dipped him in the River Styx for invulnerability but held him by the heel. That one dry spot cost him everything. The tendon in the back of your ankle is named after him.

questions.text: What is the name of the underworld river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology?
questions.explanation: Drinking from Lethe erased all memories. Dead souls drank before reincarnation. The Styx gets picked because it's more famous, but the Styx is the river of hatred, not forgetfulness.
questions.optionsJson: ["The River Cocytus", "The River Styx", "The River Acheron", "The River Lethe"]

questions.text: Who was the Roman god of war?
questions.explanation: The Greek equivalent is Ares. Mars was far more respected in Roman culture than Ares was in Greek mythology. The Romans named a planet, a month (March), and a field (Campus Martius) after him.

questions.text: In Greek mythology, who flew too close to the Sun with wax wings?
questions.explanation: His father Daedalus built the wings and warned him. Icarus ignored the warning. The story is a parable about hubris, and it's been retold for 3,000 years because the lesson never sticks.

questions.text: What mythological creature is reborn from its own ashes?
questions.explanation: Appears in Greek, Egyptian, and Chinese mythology in various forms. The lifespan varies by tradition: 500 years, 1,000 years, or 1,461 years (tied to the Sothic cycle in Egypt).

questions.text: In Norse mythology, what is the name of the world tree?
questions.explanation: An immense ash tree connecting nine worlds. Its roots reach into three wells, one guarded by a dragon. The name roughly translates to 'Odin's horse,' referring to Odin's self-sacrifice by hanging from the tree.

questions.text: Who was the Greek goddess of wisdom?
questions.explanation: Also the goddess of warfare and crafts. She sprang fully armored from Zeus's forehead after he swallowed her pregnant mother Metis. Athens is named after her.

questions.text: In Greek mythology, who is the king of the gods?
questions.explanation: Overthrew his father Kronos (who had overthrown his father Ouranos). Three generations of divine family drama. The Romans called him Jupiter.

questions.text: What creature in Egyptian mythology has the body of a lion and the head of a human?
questions.explanation: The Great Sphinx at Giza is the most famous, but sphinxes appear across Egyptian temple complexes. Greek sphinxes, by contrast, had wings and asked riddles.

questions.text: In Norse mythology, what is Ragnarök?
options: A prophesied end of the world
questions.explanation: Not just destruction. After Ragnarök, the world is reborn. Two humans survive, the earth rises from the sea, and a new cycle begins. It's apocalypse plus renewal.
questions.optionsJson: ["The creation of humankind", "A prophesied end of the world", "A god's wedding feast", "A legendary sea voyage"]

questions.text: What fictional metal is Captain America's shield made from?
questions.explanation: Adamantium is Wolverine's thing. The MCU shield is pure vibranium from Wakanda. In the original comics, it was a vibranium-steel alloy. The movies simplified it.

questions.text: In the Harry Potter series, what position does Harry play in Quidditch?
questions.explanation: Catches the Golden Snitch to end the game. Book readers nail this instantly. Film-only fans sometimes confuse it with Chaser because the movies don't explain the positions well.

questions.text: What is the name of the fictional continent in Game of Thrones?
questions.explanation: Essos is the eastern continent where Daenerys spends most of her time. People mix them up because the show bounces between both constantly.

questions.text: In Star Wars, what color is Mace Windu's lightsaber?
questions.explanation: Samuel L. Jackson specifically requested a unique color so he could spot himself in battle scenes. Every other Jedi carries blue or green. His purple blade is one of a kind in the films.

questions.text: What is the highest-grossing film of all time (not adjusted for inflation)?
questions.explanation: Titanic held the record for 12 years. Avatar took it. Avengers: Endgame briefly claimed it, then Avatar's re-release reclaimed the top spot. Gone with the Wind wins when adjusted for inflation.

questions.text: In The Lord of the Rings, what is the name of Gandalf's horse?
questions.explanation: Lord of all horses in Middle-earth, descended from Felaróf. Book fans know this cold. Movie fans remember the white horse but not the name.

questions.text: What band recorded the album 'Abbey Road'?
questions.explanation: Released in 1969. The iconic crosswalk photo on the cover is at 3 Abbey Road, London. Tourists still recreate the photo daily, blocking traffic.

questions.text: In the Mario video game series, what is Mario's brother's name?
questions.explanation: Might be the easiest question in this entire database. And yet, under time pressure in a quiz, at least one person blanks on it every time.

questions.text: What is the name of Batman's butler?
questions.explanation: Everyone says 'Alfred.' Few remember the surname. Pennyworth has been Batman's moral compass since 1943.

questions.text: Which TV show features a character named Walter White?
questions.explanation: Bryan Cranston went from the goofy dad in Malcolm in the Middle to the most terrifying chemistry teacher on television. The character's name sounds deliberately ordinary, which was the point.

questions.text: What is the name of the fictional school in the Harry Potter series?
questions.explanation: Most people say just 'Hogwarts.' Getting the full official name right is the real challenge. It's 'Witchcraft AND Wizardry,' not 'of Magic' or 'for Wizards.'

questions.text: In The Simpsons, what is Homer's favorite beer brand?
questions.explanation: Never commercially produced by the show's creators (though unauthorized versions have appeared worldwide). The name parodies generic American beer branding.

questions.text: What year was the original Super Mario Bros. released?
questions.explanation: Feels like it should be earlier. The Famicom/NES game launched in Japan in September 1985. It wasn't Mario's first appearance (that was Donkey Kong in 1981), but it was the game that defined the franchise.

questions.text: Fill in the number: ___ is the number of pounds one gallon of pure maple syrup weighs.

questions.text: Fill in the number: ___ is the number of times an average person laughs a day.

questions.text: Fill in the number: ___ is the minimum age for getting an adult job in most states and provinces across the globe.

questions.explanation: 17 is the maximum number of strokes of a Chinese radical.

questions.text: Fill in the number: ___ is the number of baby teeth in the deciduous dentition.
questions.explanation: 20 is the number of baby teeth in the deciduous dentition.

questions.text: Fill in the number: ___ is the number of chromosomes normal human sex cells have.
questions.explanation: 23 is the number of chromosomes normal human sex cells have.

questions.text: Fill in the number: ___ is the number of a car in the NASCAR Sprint Cup Series owned by Hendrick Motorsports.
questions.explanation: 24 is the number of a car in the NASCAR Sprint Cup Series owned by Hendrick Motorsports.

questions.text: Fill in the number: ___ is the number of Cantons of Switzerland.
questions.explanation: 26 is the number of Cantons of Switzerland.
